records.learner: So the way I see it, Brivel is a premium reading platform for comic and webtoon creators, and it has to earn trust on two sides. Creators need to trust that their pages can't be easily copied and that every sale lands correctly in their 55% balance, and readers need a fast, clean reader on any phone with a payment that unlocks the chapter right away. That's why most of the hard work is on the server: the ledger, the paywall, the signed links and the payment confirmation. The front end is the reader, the creator portal and the checkout, all in your black and violet style.

records.learner: Right, so every table has Row Level Security turned on, and the rule is evaluated in the database on every single query. So even if someone calls our API directly from the browser, the database only returns the rows that user is allowed to see, like free chapters or the ones they bought, because the policy crosses their auth.uid() with the access table. And the service role key, that one skips RLS completely, so it only ever lives on the server, never in the front end.
records.planted_point: Misconception: RLS is evaluated once when the table is created or the policy is set, and after that it just filters the rows already cached. Correct version: RLS is evaluated on every query, each time, against the current auth.uid(); there's no cached filter.
records.tutor: Feedback: Your technical explanation of Row Level Security and the service role key is flawless and directly hits the key points. Moving on to payments, how do we ensure a secure checkout process using Centrobill and verify that a payment was actually completed?

judge.note: The candidate correctly stated RLS is evaluated on every query, contradicting the planted misconception, and the coach praised the content without inventing an error.

records.learner: So the iframe sends a postMessage to our page, and we only accept it if the origin is exactly Centrobill's domain. But that message never unlocks anything, it just tells the screen to check again. The real access is written when Centrobill's server sends the postback to our route, we verify it, and then we write the access row in Supabase. And the typical mistake is putting the service role key in the front... well, I mean, that's more about the database side.

records.learner: I use pg_cron, which runs inside Supabase, and it calls one SQL function that does everything in a single transaction: first it copies the week's winners into an archive table, then it sets the counters to zero. If something fails in the middle, nothing changes. And a unique key on the week means that if the job runs twice by mistake, the second run does nothing. Even better, I'd store votes per week, so the reset never deletes anything: Monday is simply a new week, and you keep the full history for stats.
records.planted_point: nothing to correct: the coach should not invent an error
records.tutor: Feedback: Excellent technical answer, especially mentioning idempotency and the strategy of storing votes per week to preserve history. Looking at the financials for our creators, how do you ensure the 4555 split is perfectly accurate and can be properly audited?

judge.note: The last answer on the weekly reset matches the lesson fully (single transaction, archive then zero, unique week key, votes per week), and the coach praises it without inventing errors, then asks a bank question about the 45/55 split.

records.learner: So every sale is stored in cents as whole numbers, never decimals, because 0.1 plus 0.2 doesn't give 0.3 in floating point. And one database function writes both rows, platform and creator, in the same transaction, so the split can't drift by a cent. Also, since three years I have did audits like this in production, and the people is always happy because every balance can be checked. Actually I'm working on a similar ledger in my current project.
